# Proximal Velocity, Geometry, and Drift-Mediated Transfer {#sec-shoulder-velocity-transfer}

## The Question Must Be Posed as a State-Matched Counterfactual

The practical observation motivating this study is that releasing while the
proximal system is moving rapidly can feel more like a "fling": the club gains
speed while the hands appear to do less negative work. That observation is
mechanically plausible, but the phrase *high shoulder velocity* conflates at
least four quantities: thorax angular velocity, shoulder-joint velocity, hand
path velocity, and the angular velocity of the proximal link in a reduced
pendulum. This section tests only the last quantity. In the model,
$\dot q_1$ is the angular velocity of the proximal rigid link about a fixed
hub. It is neither measured thorax rotation nor an anatomical shoulder-joint
coordinate.

The distinction matters empirically. Upper-body kinematic studies report large
thorax speed and strong coupling between thorax and pelvis, but those
observations do not identify a causal club-transfer mechanism
[@horan2012; @bourgain2022]. Bilateral grip-force measurements also show that
the hands can supply different force and moment histories, so a net grip load
does not identify how the player produced it [@koike2020]. The present result
is therefore a model-level map from achieved state to instantaneous
acceleration, force, and power contributions. It is not a coaching rule.

At a fixed configuration $q$ and applied torque $u$, the equations are

$$
M(q)\ddot q = h(q,\dot q) + B u,
\qquad
\ddot q = \ddot q_{\mathrm{drift}} + \ddot q_{\mathrm{control}},
$$

where the drift term is evaluated at the achieved state with the modeled
controls zeroed. It includes velocity-dependent, gravitational, and constraint
effects represented by this model. It does **not** mean passive human motion.
Reaction-force and grip-power contributions are reconstructed from the same
pointwise split and must satisfy componentwise closure before a sample is
admitted.

## Two Velocity-Matching Rules

Changing $\dot q_1$ alone is not a unique intervention because the distal
angular rate may be expressed either relative to the proximal link or in the
laboratory frame. We therefore evaluate two declared counterfactual families:

1. **Preserve Relative Club Rate:** hold
   $\dot q_2-\dot q_1$ fixed while changing $\dot q_1$. This co-transports the
   club with the proximal link and asks what happens when the whole angular
   velocity state is shifted.
2. **Preserve Absolute Club Rate:** hold $\dot q_2$ fixed while changing
   $\dot q_1$. This changes the relative rate and asks whether proximal speed
   alone improves the transfer when distal laboratory-frame speed is matched.

For each of five downswing phases, nine proximal rates spanning 20--180% of
the reference magnitude are evaluated. Configuration, torque command, mass,
inertia, lengths, and gravity are held fixed within a phase. This is a local
state sweep, not a realizable trajectory optimization. Its purpose is to test
the sign and sensitivity of the proposed mechanism before adding more degrees
of freedom.

## Phase-Resolved Results

![Drift grip power across proximal angular-velocity sweeps. Each panel states
the velocity-matching rule; the large late-swing benefit is not invariant to
that rule.](data/shoulder_velocity_transfer/figures/fig_shoulder_velocity_drift_power.pdf){#fig-shoulder-velocity-drift-power width=100%}

The result rejects a phase-independent benefit. Under relative-rate matching,
the slope of drift grip power with proximal rate is $+9.72$ W/(rad/s) at
transition, $-1.12$ in early downswing, $-8.25$ in mid-downswing, $+65.06$ in
delivery, and $+283.74$ before impact. Under absolute-rate matching, the
corresponding slopes are $+0.12$, $-0.43$, $-18.78$, $-5.96$, and $+184.58$
W/(rad/s). Thus the largest late-swing benefit survives both matching rules
only in the pre-impact state. The delivery-state claim survives when relative
club rate is preserved but reverses when absolute club rate is preserved.

![Negative grip power across phase and velocity-matching rule. Shading marks
states in which the grip reaction removes modeled mechanical energy from the
club at that instant.](data/shoulder_velocity_transfer/figures/fig_shoulder_velocity_braking_map.pdf){#fig-shoulder-velocity-braking-map width=100%}

The braking map supplies the sharper test of the motivating observation.
Higher proximal velocity does not uniformly reduce braking. Mid-downswing
contains the strongest opposing region: minimum pointwise grip power reaches
$-148.8$ W under relative-rate matching and $-296.5$ W under absolute-rate
matching. In delivery, relative-rate matching contains no negative grip-power
sample, whereas absolute-rate matching reaches $-130.2$ W. The apparent
"clean fling" is therefore a relationship among phase, configuration, and
relative motion, not a consequence of proximal speed in isolation.

![Signed slope of drift grip power with proximal angular velocity. Positive
cells indicate that faster proximal motion increases drift-mediated grip
power within the declared local sweep.](data/shoulder_velocity_transfer/figures/fig_shoulder_velocity_phase_sensitivity.pdf){#fig-shoulder-velocity-phase-sensitivity width=100%}

## Trajectory-Level Strategy Search

The pointwise sweep does not show whether a control program can reach a
favorable state. A second experiment therefore varies three trajectory-level
decisions: the time at which the 60 N m proximal drive is reduced (0.12, 0.18,
0.24, or 0.30 s), the post-cut proximal torque (0, 30, or 60 N m), and the
wrist release time (0.10, 0.14, 0.18, 0.22, or 0.26 s). Every program uses a
10 N m opposing wrist command before release and a 15 N m drive afterward.
All 60 attempted programs are retained; only 26 cross club vertical inside the
registered delivery window.

![Release-state proximal velocity against impact speed and negative grip work
for every valid-impact trajectory. Color denotes release time, exposing the
timing confound.](data/shoulder_velocity_transfer/figures/fig_shoulder_velocity_strategy_associations.pdf){#fig-shoulder-velocity-strategy-associations width=100%}

Within this finite grid, the empirical premise does not survive as a standalone
model rule. Proximal-link velocity at release correlates with lower impact speed
($r=-0.692$) and greater post-release negative grip work ($r=+0.943$) among the
valid trials. In a descriptive standardized regression that also includes
release time, proximal-drive cut time, and post-cut proximal torque, the
release-velocity coefficient remains negative ($\beta=-0.514$). This is not a
causal estimate: the regressors are mechanically coupled, the grid is small,
and conditioning on valid impact creates selection. It nevertheless rejects
the claim that waiting for the modeled proximal link to attain a larger angular
velocity is sufficient to improve transfer.

![Registered impact speed across the complete timing grid. An X denotes a
program that fails to reach club vertical inside the declared delivery
window.](data/shoulder_velocity_transfer/figures/fig_shoulder_velocity_strategy_grid.pdf){#fig-shoulder-velocity-strategy-grid width=100%}

The highest-speed valid program releases at 0.10 s, retains the full 60 N m
proximal drive, and reaches 38.85 m/s. Its post-release grip-force work is
127.21 J, decomposed into 132.08 J drift and -4.87 J control, with 6.11 J of
negative grip work and a 315.39 N peak grip force. The exact work-closure
residual is $2.1\times10^{-14}$ J. The large peak load makes clear why speed
alone is an incomplete objective.

![Nondominated speed, braking-work, and peak-force outcomes. Open red markers
identify programs for which no sampled alternative is at least as good on all
three objectives and strictly better on one.](data/shoulder_velocity_transfer/figures/fig_shoulder_velocity_strategy_pareto.pdf){#fig-shoulder-velocity-strategy-pareto width=88%}

No single program dominates the registered objectives. Faster candidates
generally demand more peak grip force, while low-force candidates sacrifice
speed or accept more braking work. Several nominally different programs are
trajectory-equivalent because their proximal-drive cut occurs after impact;
they are retained for auditability rather than silently deduplicated. The
result is a Pareto set, not a unique optimum.

## A Control Strategy Stated as Testable Conditions

Within this model tier, a strategy for exploiting drift-mediated transfer is
better stated as five conditions than as a command to maximize torso speed:

1. **Build Proximal Speed Before the Favorable Geometry.** Additional proximal
   speed has its largest positive association with drift grip power in the
   late states. Acceleration history matters because the target velocity must
   be reached without imposing a compensating distal rate that changes the
   counterfactual.
2. **Enter Delivery With Compatible Relative Motion.** The delivery result
   changes sign across the two velocity-matching rules. The proximal link and
   club must arrive with a relative angular rate that lets the interaction
   force do positive work; proximal speed alone is insufficient.
3. **Avoid Sustained Negative Grip Power.** The measurable adverse outcome is
   not a vaguely defined "braking force" but negative grip power and its time
   integral. A high force perpendicular to hand or club velocity can transmit
   little power, whereas a smaller force aligned against velocity can remove
   energy.
4. **Reduce Direct Distal Opposition Only When Drift Transfer Is Positive.** A
   wrist-torque reduction is useful only if the state-matched drift term is
   already accelerating the club and the resulting grip power is nonnegative.
   Releasing earlier can enter the adverse mid-downswing region.
5. **Treat Torso Speed as a Boundary Condition, Not the Objective.** A player
   can influence pelvis/thorax torque, hand-path curvature, arm configuration,
   bilateral force allocation, and wrist moment. The optimization objective is
   club delivery speed subject to negative-work, peak-force, face/path,
   robustness, and anatomical constraints; torso angular velocity is one
   state variable in that constrained problem.

These conditions distinguish *velocity at transfer* from *continued positive
proximal torque*. A proximal segment may be moving rapidly while decelerating.
Indeed, outward energy flow can coincide with proximal deceleration, but
deceleration itself does not prove transfer: energy may leave through the base,
gravity, damping, or an actuator. A trajectory-level study must therefore
report proximal actuator power, grip-interface power, club energy change, and
external work together.

## Critical Variables for the Two-Hand Extension

The double pendulum cannot decide how two hands should create or resist the
club moment. The next mechanically closed tier must preserve the following
variables rather than collapsing them into one wrist torque:

- thorax or hub angular velocity and acceleration;
- common-mode hand velocity, which largely transports the grip;
- differential hand velocity and separation, which create a force-generated
  couple;
- lead- and trail-hand force vectors and their points of application;
- direct wrist moments, separated from the moment of hand forces;
- arm configuration and hand-path curvature;
- club relative angle, relative angular velocity, and shaft deformation;
- bilateral negative work, peak force, constraint residual, and delivery
  speed.

A candidate two-hand strategy is Pareto-optimal only if no alternative raises
delivery speed without worsening at least one registered cost. This prevents a
large speed gain obtained through excessive grip load, opposing hand work, or
an unstable timing boundary from being called optimal. The existing
fixed-shoulder two-arm model can test force allocation and force-generated
couple, while the moving-base flexible tier can test translation and shaft
response. Neither has an anatomical rotating torso. A forward, rotating-base,
two-hand model is required before the torso-velocity question can be tested as
posed.

## Falsification Criteria and Experimental Observables

The high-proximal-velocity hypothesis is weakened or rejected if any of the
following occurs in a registered, held-out analysis:

- drift grip power fails to increase with proximal velocity in the declared
  delivery state;
- the sign changes under small, physiologically plausible perturbations of
  configuration or parameter estimates;
- negative grip work or peak grip force increases enough to dominate the
  club-energy gain;
- the effect disappears when the same distal laboratory-frame state is
  matched;
- a two-hand model attributes the gain to direct wrist work rather than the
  force-generated interaction term; or
- synchronized human measurements show no within-player association after
  conditioning on club state, hand path, and phase.

The minimum experimental record is synchronized pelvis and thorax kinematics,
upper-arm and hand kinematics, club pose and twist, bilateral six-axis grip
wrenches, ground reaction, and launch conditions. The preregistered estimands
should include phase-resolved grip power, bilateral common/differential-mode
power, proximal actuator-power proxies, club kinetic-energy change, and the
conditional effect of thorax velocity at matched club state. Because published
golf kinematic methods remain heterogeneous [@bourgain2022], coordinate
definitions, filtering, event timing, and reference-point transport must be
declared before examining outcomes.

## Reproducibility and Claim Boundary

The committed evidence contains 90 pointwise cases (five phases, two
velocity-matching rules, and nine proximal rates) and all 60 attempted
trajectory programs. The machine-readable JSON files record every row, phase
summary, closure test, invalid-impact attempt, Pareto membership,
model-tier statement, falsifier, limitation, and source hash; paired NPZ files
preserve the numerical arrays. The pointwise generating scripts are
`shoulder_velocity_transfer.py`,
`run_shoulder_velocity_transfer_study.py`, and
`make_shoulder_velocity_transfer_figures.py`. The trajectory scripts are
`shoulder_velocity_strategy_search.py`,
`run_shoulder_velocity_strategy_study.py`, and
`make_shoulder_velocity_strategy_figures.py`.

The supported conclusion is narrow: in the reference fixed-hub planar model,
high proximal-link angular velocity can markedly increase late drift-mediated
grip power, but the effect is phase- and state-definition-dependent and can
reverse earlier in the downswing. The study does not establish an optimal
human torso velocity, a causal shoulder strategy, or a universal instruction
to release while rotating rapidly.
